title: What If a Skyscraper Could Tip Over in a Storm? New York Had One in 1978

scenes.text: What if a new skyscraper could fall over in a storm? In 1978, one in Manhattan could.
Citicorp Center, 59 storeys, finished in 1977. To fit over a church, it stands on stilts at the middle of each side, not the corners.
In 1978 a student calls the engineer: what about wind hitting the corners? He had only checked the faces.
He redoes the maths. A storm able to topple it hits New York every 55 years or so. If a blackout stops the building's damper: every 16.
All summer, welders reinforce the joints at night and vanish before the office workers arrive. Police plan a ten-block evacuation.
Hurricane Ella heads up the coast, then turns out to sea. The newspapers were on strike. No one found out for 17 years.

description:
What if a skyscraper had a hidden fatal flaw? Citicorp Center in Manhattan, completed in 1977, stands on nine-storey stilts set at the midpoints of its sides so it could rise over St. Peter's Lutheran Church. In 1978 an undergraduate, Diane Hartley, questioned structural engineer William LeMessurier about quartering winds hitting the corners, which his calculations had not covered.
LeMessurier found that a storm able to topple the building struck New York roughly every 55 years with the tuned mass damper running, or every 16 years if a blackout stopped it. Crews welded reinforcements over the joints each night, the NYPD prepared a 10-block evacuation plan, 2,500 Red Cross volunteers were on standby, and three weather services watched Hurricane Ella, which never made landfall. With New York's newspapers on strike, the story stayed secret until The New Yorker published it in 1995.
